title: What is Redux
description: Understand Redux and its place in React applications.

data.text: **Redux** is a predictable state container for JavaScript applications. It helps you write applications that behave consistently, run in different environments (client, server, and native), and are easy to test. At its core, Redux is a pattern for managing state that is independent of any UI framework, though it is most commonly used with React.

data.title: Framework-Agnostic
data.text: Redux is not tied to React. You can use it with Angular, Vue, Svelte, or even plain JavaScript. React-Redux is the official binding layer for React components.

As your application grows, passing state down through props and lifting it up to shared parents becomes painful. Redux provides a single store that any component can connect to, eliminating prop drilling and making state changes predictable.

data.title: Key Benefits
items: **Predictable**: State changes follow strict, traceable rules
**Centralized**: All state lives in one place, the store
**Flexible**: Works with any UI layer or no UI at all
**Maintainable**: Clear separation between state and view logic

data.text: Redux is most valuable in larger applications with complex shared state. For a small app with local component state, the boilerplate may not be worth it. Consider Redux when you have:

data.title: Good Use Cases
items: Large amounts of application state shared across many components
State that is updated frequently from many places
Complex state update logic that benefits from being centralized
A large codebase with many developers needing clear patterns
Need for time-travel debugging or state persistence

data.text: Redux follows a **unidirectional data flow**. State always flows in one direction: from the store to the view, and changes flow back through actions and reducers. This loop is at the heart of every Redux application.

cards.title: Redux
cards.description: Centralized store, predictable updates, time-travel debugging, framework-agnostic.

cards.title: React Context
cards.description: Built into React, no extra library. Good for low-frequency updates like theme or locale.

cards.title: MobX
cards.description: Reactive observables that automatically track dependencies. Less boilerplate than Redux.

cards.title: Zustand
cards.description: Minimalist state management with a hooks-based API. Growing in popularity.

The method used to send an action to the store, triggering a state update.

data.title: Modern Redux
data.text: Today, the official recommended way to write Redux is with **Redux Toolkit** (RTK). RTK removes most of the boilerplate and includes best practices by default, so you should start there rather than the bare createStore API.

data.title: Trace the Data Flow
data.description: Given a small app with a counter, trace what happens when a user clicks an increment button.
steps: Sketch the data flow as a sequence of steps
Identify which object holds the state at each step
Explain why the UI updates after the reducer returns
Now mentally apply the same flow to a real-world feature, like adding an item to a cart
data.expectedOutcome: You can clearly explain how an action flows from the view through the reducer back to the view, and you can apply the same mental model to any Redux feature.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Redux is a predictable, centralized state container
It is framework-agnostic but commonly used with React
It follows a strict unidirectional data flow
Best for complex apps with shared state
Modern Redux uses Redux Toolkit for less boilerplate
data.takeaway: Redux provides predictable, centralized state management for complex JavaScript applications.
